title: AI costs: Time savings obscure delivery economics
desc: Shifts pricing analysis toward total cost and consumption visibility, while fixed fees and client pass-throughs leave valuation unresolved.

kps.k: Legal AI shifts the economic question from time saved to the total cost of delivering work.
kps.d: Shaver argues that document-heavy workflows consume substantial tokens and that AI’s integration into client delivery will require continuing investment in technology, people and supporting resources. Pereyra reports that more useful models encourage greater adoption and longer runs, citing $20 drafting queries and $20,000 review jobs as examples, not average costs. Nuara reports falling token prices but increasing agentic activity over the preceding two years. Together, these accounts distinguish cheaper units of computation from lower overall spending; they do not establish that substituting AI for human work automatically improves margins.

qs.q: So I think the key question is more: how will the investment over time make sense within the firm’s business model, and how will firms be able to accommodate the ongoing investment?
qs.a: Is Legal Tech in a Bubble? — Nikki Shaver · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: Um they're using more tokens because they're running for longer and they work so much better that users are using them more.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: the legal agent benchmark and the coming token-pricing reckoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Consumption pricing exposes costs that bundled licences can obscure, but its eventual dominance remains a forecast.
kps.d: Shaver says legal applications currently negotiate with model providers and offer broadly unlimited usage within licences; her example of firms routing Claude-related work through Harvey to save money is anecdotal. Stephanie Wilkins, in the opening remarks to the Buckley interview, reports Legora’s move to consumption pricing for Agent Pro and predicts others will follow. These accounts describe different commercial arrangements, not a uniform market transition. Pereyra warns that consumption billing creates accountability problems of its own and may give providers incentives to increase token use.

qs.q: So you’re actually getting away with something by using the legal applications, because at the moment they take on the negotiation with the frontier model labs.
qs.a: Is Legal Tech in a Bubble? — Nikki Shaver · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: Recently, Legora also announced that it’s moving its Agent Pro offering  Consumption based pricing, which means it’s billing by what the agent does rather than by a flat seat license.
qs.a: AI Is Shifting the Bottleneck: Actionstep’s Triona Buckley on Building Smarter Mid-Market Law Firms · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Forecasts diverge over how quickly efficiency and competition will relieve cost pressure.
kps.d: Lambert predicts token costs will stop being a major issue within two or three years as efficiencies and competition develop; Gebauer agrees while stressing the immediate burden. Shaver likewise expects lower costs or backend efficiencies, but still anticipates growing technology investment. By contrast, the ILTACON report attributes to Weinberg a forecast of continued frontier-model price increases because data-centre and power constraints limit additional capacity before 2029. Pereyra sees competition and specialised models as potential constraints on cost, not achieved solutions. These predictions address different drivers—unit prices, infrastructure, usage and total investment—and the excerpts do not resolve their net effect.

qs.q: Marlene Gebauer (43:22)  It’s a significant short-term issue.
qs.a: From AI Personas to Rogue Agents: Rethinking Legal Training, Security, and Value · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: So my sense is that ultimately token costs will also come down or there will be new efficiency means where it it won't be as significant and it won't certainly won't sit with us.
qs.a: Nikki Shaver — Legaltech Hub (agentic governance and the efficacy turn) · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Cost visibility attracts broad support, while responsibility for optimisation remains unsettled.
kps.d: Nuara describes Deal Driver’s clause- and run-level cost tracking and model comparisons, and recommends incorporating tool costs into transaction economics and fee quotes. Pereyra anticipates detailed agent-spending explanations and proposes task benchmarking and routing. Wilkins highlights immediate user practices such as avoiding duplicate document submissions and unnecessarily prolonged chats. Shaver accepts current token-management guidance but argues that software, rather than lawyers, should eventually handle optimisation. The tension concerns the duration and location of the burden, not whether costs matter. Product descriptions and proposed controls do not demonstrate measured savings.

qs.q: Her model that you’re spending so you can call up that you looked at document X and you can see that you’ve ran 14 different agentic flows and what the cost of each run is for the clause in that one document.
qs.a: Flatiron Law Group's Lennie Nuara on Talent-First AI, M&A Workflows, and the Future of Legal Practice · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: It's like, well, we can help you benchmark that and route all these and say, oh, actually for this task, you don't need to use all these tokens.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: the legal agent benchmark and the coming token-pricing reckoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Neither passing costs to clients nor switching to fixed fees resolves the valuation problem.
kps.d: Gebauer questions per-token pricing and cautions against automatic client pass-through, invoking clients’ eventual resistance to Lexis and Westlaw charges as overhead. She recommends distinguishing client value from benefits that accrue only internally to the firm. Pereyra challenges expectations that fixed fees will necessarily protect margins: pricing complex work engagement by engagement creates valuation and negotiation burdens, whereas hourly billing supplies a scalable convention. Speaker 2 in Inside Harvey also expects hourly billing to persist. These arguments favour attention to value and accountability without establishing a single preferred pricing model.

qs.q: And I mean, look, in the beginning that made very good sense, but you know, in time it became a situation where clients said, look, that’s the cost of doing business and we’re not gonna pay for that.
qs.a: From AI Personas to Rogue Agents: Rethinking Legal Training, Security, and Value · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: And I think the problem you run into of pricing the work is actually the same problem that law firms run into when they try to do fixed fee pricing, right?
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: the legal agent benchmark and the coming token-pricing reckoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: ROI requires accounting for human verification and service quality, not just adoption or gross time savings.
kps.d: The ILTACON report and Buckley say continuing human review reduces efficiency gains and cost recovery, without quantifying that burden. Speaker 1 in Inside Harvey reports that a late-2025 Wharton study found strong legal-sector adoption growth but weak ROI measurement; the excerpt supplies no methods or figures. The speaker separately attributes measurement difficulty to legal teams’ emphasis on thoroughness and avoiding mistakes. An interviewer’s report of roughly 37 hours saved monthly by law-firm power users does not establish net financial returns or causation. The practical implication is to connect workflow-level spending with review effort and client outcomes; proposed team-wide tracking and audit trails remain capabilities or recommendations rather than proven ROI improvements.

qs.q: Actionstep’s chief product officer [Triona Buckley](https://nz.linkedin.com/in/trionabuckleysaunders) noted that firms have not yet fully realised efficiency gains because significant human review remains necessary.
qs.a: ILTACON 2026: Context is King — But Transformation is Still the Hard Part · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: First of all, there's this amazing study from Wharton at the end of 2025 that showed that legal increase, it was the biggest increase in usage of AI from all the verticals, but they were the worst at measuring ROI.
qs.a: E50 - Inside Harvey with Winston Weinberg, Founder & CEO of Harvey · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The traditional-law-firm source accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that gross time savings and declining token prices do not by themselves establish improved delivery economics. Nuara materially extends it by specifying an operational response: track AI consumption at the clause and agentic-run level, aggregate it across matters, compare model costs, and incorporate tool expenditure into transaction economics and fee quotes. His position combines optimism that AI will perform assigned work far more efficiently with caution that expanding agentic usage and opaque vendor charges can offset cheaper unit costs. The source therefore strengthens the cluster’s emphasis on total-cost visibility rather than opposing AI adoption. Materially, however, the evidence consists of Nuara’s experience, forecasts and descriptions of Deal Driver’s capabilities; it does not demonstrate realised savings, improved margins or ROI. Because the curated evidence contains only one law-firm source, it does not establish how widely this view is shared within traditional practice.

qs.q: Now, my experience has been at least the past two years, the token cost is going down, but the usage of how many agentic events that you have is going up.
qs.a: Flatiron Law Group's Lennie Nuara on Talent-First AI, M&A Workflows, and the Future of Legal Practice · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: And the cost of a tool is part of the economics of the transaction and how you quote.
qs.a: Flatiron Law Group's Lennie Nuara on Talent-First AI, M&A Workflows, and the Future of Legal Practice · Law firms · 2026

vlens.an: Across this curated legal-tech-vendor set, the sources accept the proposition that gross time savings are an inadequate measure of legal AI economics and collectively develop it with concrete accounts of consumption, cost visibility and valuation. Common reasons are that better-performing systems can induce more and longer usage; seat licences may hide underlying consumption; and legal ROI is difficult to reduce to efficiency because service quality, thoroughness and error avoidance also matter. Pereyra makes the strongest extension: he argues that consumption billing creates its own accountability and optimisation requirements, while fixed fees reproduce the valuation and negotiation problems that help sustain hourly billing. The Inside Harvey discussion reinforces team-level token tracking and the persistence of hourly billing, but frames vertical vendors’ ROI advantage as prospective. Wilkins is narrower and more operational, reporting Legora’s pricing change and recommending user-level token discipline; her forecast that other providers will follow is not evidence of a market-wide transition. Thus, the material variation concerns how costs should be controlled and priced—not whether delivery economics and consumption visibility matter—and none of these selected sources establishes measured net savings or a settled pricing model.

qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: the legal agent benchmark and the coming token-pricing reckoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: And I think the problem you run into of pricing the work is actually the same problem that law firms run into when they try to do fixed fee pricing, right?
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: the legal agent benchmark and the coming token-pricing reckoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources support the proposition that gross time savings are an inadequate measure of legal AI economics. Their common reasoning is that firms must account for model consumption, continuing technology investment, surrounding personnel and resources, human verification, and the client value actually delivered. They also question whether usage charges can simply be passed through to clients. Material variation concerns future cost trajectories and who should optimise consumption: Shaver expects backend efficiencies and argues that token management should eventually move out of lawyers’ hands; Lambert and Gebauer predict competition will ease token pressure after a significant near-term burden; the ILTACON report instead relays forecasts of rising frontier-model prices under infrastructure constraints. These are divergent predictions rather than disagreement with the principal proposition, and none establishes that lower unit costs, fixed fees, or adoption alone will produce favourable margins or measurable ROI.

qs.q: So I think the key question is more: how will the investment over time make sense within the firm’s business model, and how will firms be able to accommodate the ongoing investment?
qs.a: Is Legal Tech in a Bubble? — Nikki Shaver · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: Despite substantial AI adoption, many organisations are still wrestling with a ‘verification tax’ that takes away from time savings, meaning that firms are doubling up on effort and time and not recouping costs.
qs.a: ILTACON 2026: Context is King — But Transformation is Still the Hard Part · Market & press · 2026

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively support the proposition that headline time savings and falling token prices are insufficient measures of legal AI economics. Their common reasoning is that total delivery cost also includes expanding agentic consumption, sustained investment in technology and supporting personnel, and continuing human verification; accordingly, favourable margins or ROI cannot be inferred from gross efficiency claims. They also broadly favour greater consumption visibility and connecting AI expenditure to transaction economics, pricing and client value. Material variation concerns what happens next rather than the core proposition: Nuara and Pereyra develop granular tracking, benchmarking and routing responses; Shaver expects optimisation increasingly to move into software while overall investment rises; Lambert and Gebauer forecast that efficiency and competition will ease token-cost pressure within two or three years; the ILTACON account instead reports a forecast of rising frontier-model prices because of infrastructure constraints. The sources also differ over commercial mechanisms—bundled licences versus consumption pricing, client pass-through, fixed fees and continued hourly billing—but none treats a change in pricing unit as resolving valuation. These conclusions describe only the supplied curated sources and do not establish how prevalent the views are in the wider legal sector.
